aflcio_description: The Senate's Rule 22 requires a two-thirds vote to stop a filibuster. Because of this, the Senate has been unable to act on repeal of Taft-Hartley's Sec. 14(b) and major civil rights bills. The filibuster has also been used to block any change in the rule. On Jan. 24, 1967, the Senate voted 53-46 for Majority Leader Mansfield's motion to close debate on the rules change, but it was defeated for lack of a two-thirds margin. Yea - right. Nay - wrong.

Sen. Ralph Yarborough sought to balance the compulsory arbitration bill by an amendment impounding 10 percent of the railroads' profits during the period in which rail workers were prohibited from striking - thus creating an incentive for a voluntary settlement of the dispute. The amendment was rejected, 23-59, on June 7, 1967. Yea - right. Nay - wrong.

A House-passed bill would have allowed states to evade one man-one vote standards for congressional districts until 1972. An amendment by Sen. Edward Kennedy (D-Mass.) strengthened the bill by limiting the population variation to no more than 10 percent, beginning with 1968 elections, and barring gerrymandering. It was adopted, 44-39, on June 8, 1967. Yea - right. Nay - wrong.

The Teachers Corps sends trained teaching teams to poverty areas where educational needs are greatest. An amendment by Sen. Morse (D-Ore.) to raise its appropriations from $18 million to the $33 million asked by Pres. Johnson was rejected, 43-45, on Aug. 2, 1967. Yea - right. Nay - wrong.

An amendment by Sen. Robert Kennedy (D-N.Y.) to authorize an additional $72 million for the Alliance for Progress would have helped the growth of democratic trade unions in Latin America through additional support for the programs of the American Institute for Free Labor Development. It was rejected, 38-53, on Aug. 17, 1967. Yea - right. Nay - wrong.

A 21-nation agreement was jeopardized when Sen. Lausche (D-Ohio) sought to cut $150 million from increased special project funds for the Inter-American Bank, designed to raise living standards and strengthen Latin American economies. The Lausche amendment was rejected, 38-41, on Aug. 24, 1967. Yea - wrong. Nay - right.

An amendment by Sen. Williams (R-Del.) to an election reform bill was aimed at the AFL-CIO Committee on Political Education. It would have prevented COPE from giving dollars voluntarily contributed by union members to endorsed candidates for Congress. The amendment was rejected, 19-46, on Sept. 11, 1967. Yea - wrong. Nay - right.

aflcio_description: Funds for rent supplements, to help poor families live in decent housing, would have been cut in half under an amendment proposed by Sen. Lausche (D-Ohio). It was rejected, 34-55, on Sept. 20, 1967. Yea - wrong. Nay - right.

A labor-supported proposal by Sen. Prouty (R-Vt.) would have set up a one-year, $925 million emergency job program - a step in the direction of the large-scale job program urged by the AFL-CIO and the Urban Coalition. It was rejected, 42-47, on Oct. 4, 1967. Yea - right. Nay - wrong.

Big California growers wanted Gov. Reagan to be able to veto community anti-poverty programs assisting migrant workers which might aid farm workers' organizing efforts. An amendment by Sen. Murphy (R-Calif.) to accomplish this was rejected, 41-45, on Oct. 4, 1967. Yea - wrong. Nay - right.
Sen. Williams (R-Del.) sought to cut $198 million from the anti-poverty bill in the Senate. His amendment was rejected, 36-50, on Oct. 5, 1967. Yea - wrong. Nay - right.

The Senate social security bill was greatly superior to the House-passed bill. An amendment by Sen. Curtis (R-Neb.) would have reduced benefits to the level of the House bill. It was rejected, 22-58, on Nov. 21, 1967. Yea - wrong. Nay - right.
A "states' rights" amendment to give control of federal school funds to state boards of education was rejected, 35-38, on Dec. 11, 1967. For - wrong; Against - right.

A filibuster against the fair housing civil rights bill was broken when a motion to limit debate received the necessary two-thirds majority. The vote to end the filibuster was 65-32, on Mar. 4, 1968. For - right; Against - wrong.

aflcio_description: Pre-school children have been helped to overcome poverty handicaps through the Head Start program. An amendment by Sen. Clark (D-Pa.) to appropriate $25 million for Head Start was approved, 43-42, on Mar. 11, 1968 - after Vice Pres. Humphrey cast the tie-breaking vote. For - right; Against - wrong.

Many cities have used tax-exempt industrial bonds to finance plants as a lure to runaway industry - along with low wages and a non-union workforce. The Senate on Mar. 28, 1968, voted 50-32 to end this tax exemption. For - right; Against - wrong.

A House-Senate conference committee recommended knocking out $75 million for the 1968 summer youth manpower training programs and $25 million from Head Start. The conference report was rejected, 24-54, on Apr. 10, 1968. For - wrong; Against - right.

corrections: tally 53-45 -> 45-53 per Voteview roll 5; the card prints a defeated proposal's tally majority-first
aflcio_description: The Senate muffed a chance to change its filibuster rule at the start of the 91st Congress. Shortly before he left office, Vice Pres. Humphrey ruled that only a majority vote was needed to act on a change in the Senate's rules at the start of a new Congress. If the Senate had sustained this ruling when it was appealed, the power of a minority to keep the majority from acting on legislation could have been curbed. But on Jan. 16, 1969, the Senate refused to sustain Humphrey's ruling by a 53-45 vote. For - right. Against - wrong.

Millions of poor Americans are ill-fed. A proposal by Sen. McGovern (D-S.D.) called for free food stamps for families with monthly incomes under $60 and authorized $1.25 billion for this program for fiscal 1970. The proposal was accepted 54-40, Sept. 24, 1969. For - right. Against - wrong.

Conservatives opposed to the war on poverty sought to give governors absolute veto power over legal services projects for the poor. A proposal by Sen. Murphy (R-Calif.) to this effect was approved 45-40, Oct. 14, 1969. For - wrong. Against - right. (Murphy's amendment was later knocked out of the final bill.)

corrections: tally 36-34 -> 34-36 per Voteview roll 126; the card prints a defeated proposal's tally majority-first
aflcio_description: Many progressive programs have suffered deep fund cuts during 1969, among them programs to aid our choked, blighted cities. Sen. Hart (D-Mich.) tried to increase appropriations for urban renewal by $587.5 million. His proposal was rejected 36-34, Nov. 10, 1969. For - right. Against - wrong.

corrections: tally 55-45 -> 45-55 per Voteview roll 135; the card prints a defeated proposal's tally majority-first. Date Nov. 21, 1969 kept against Voteview's 1969-11-13: senate.gov's Supreme Court nominations table and this newspaper's own report of the vote both give Nov. 21, a Friday
aflcio_description: A consistent pattern of anti-union decisions, hostility to civil rights progress and gross insensitivity to conflicts of interest led the AFL-CIO and civil rights groups to oppose Pres. Nixon's nomination of Judge Clement F. Haynsworth, Jr., to the Supreme Court. On Nov. 21, 1969, the Senate rejected the nomination by a 55-45 vote. For - wrong. Against - right.

The $600 personal income tax exemption has been long outdated and is obviously inadequate. As a major measure of tax reform - one of the biggest issues in Congress and the nation - Sen. Gore (D-Tenn.) proposed increasing the personal exemption to $800. The Senate approved the Gore amendment 58-37, Dec. 3, 1969. For - right. Against - wrong. (The final bill changed this to a three-step increase to $750.)

corrections: tally 53-35 -> 52-36 per Voteview roll 150; one vote is on the wrong side of the dash, the total being 88 either way
aflcio_description: Some tax-exempt foundations help to finance voter registration activity, particularly among the rural and urban poor. They can continue to do so, for non-partisan registration drives carried on in two or more states, thanks to an amendment by Sen. Yarborough (D-Tex.). It was approved 53-35, Dec. 4, 1969. For - right. Against - wrong.

corrections: tally 52-24 -> 24-52 per Voteview roll 165; the card prints a defeated proposal's tally majority-first
aflcio_description: For years, many wealthy individuals have ducked taxation entirely or, by using various tax loopholes, have paid absurdly little. Sen. Kennedy (D-Mass.) proposed a four-bracket graduated minimum tax to get a fair share of these escaping dollars in place of the inadequate five percent minimum tax approved by the Senate Finance Committee. However, the Kennedy proposal was rejected 52-24, Dec. 6, 1969. For - right. Against - wrong.

corrections: tally 59-27 -> 27-59 per Voteview roll 171; the card prints a defeated proposal's tally majority-first
aflcio_description: Prompted by the National Right to Work Committee, Sen. Fannin (R-Ariz.) introduced an amendment to the tax bill to deny tax exemptions to presently exempt organizations which engage in political activities, even non-partisan registration drives. The Fannin proposal was aimed squarely at the labor movement. The amendment was rejected 59-27, Dec. 8, 1969. For - wrong. Against - right.

Congressional conservatives have steadily chipped away at funding for the war on poverty, reducing the effectiveness of its programs. An amendment by Sen. Nelson (D-Wis.), adding $400 million to the amount the Appropriations Committee had recommended, was approved 60-32, Dec. 16, 1969. For - right. Against - wrong.

The House passed an amendment to prevent cutting federal funds to school districts refusing to desegregate. Despite Supreme Court decisions, the House plan said federal funds could not be denied school districts permitting so-called "freedom of choice" plans. Sen. Scott (R-Pa.) proposed an amendment to nullify the House action, and the Senate approved it, 52-37, Dec. 17, 1969. For - right. Against - wrong. (The House subsequently concurred. See House vote No. 9.)

A proposal by Sen. Javits (R-N.Y.) was approved to provide free school lunches to children from families with incomes of less than $4,000. A move to reconsider the vote and give opponents a chance to kill the proposal was rejected, Feb. 24, 1970, 39-42. For - wrong. Against - right.

Sen. Hruska (R-Neb.) carried the ball for Nixon Administration efforts to water down the 1965 Voting Rights Act in the Senate. He moved to table, thus kill, a proposal to extend the present act for five years. Hruska's motion was defeated Mar. 5, 1970, 32-47. For - wrong. Against right.

A proposal by Sen. Mondale (D-Minn.) to provide unemployment insurance coverage for migrant farm workers was approved Apr. 7, 1970, 42-36. For - Right. Against - wrong. (Subsequent House action knocked out coverage for any farm workers.)

corrections: tally 51-45 -> 45-51 per Voteview roll 357; the card prints a defeated proposal's tally majority-first. Date Apr. 8, 1970 kept against Voteview's 1970-04-07: senate.gov's Supreme Court nominations table and this newspaper's own report of the vote, printed with the full roll of names, both give Apr. 8
aflcio_description: Following the rejection of Judge Haynsworth's nomination, Pres. Nixon submitted the name of G. Harrold Carswell as his nominee to the Supreme Court. Like Haynsworth, Carswell had a long record of insensitivity to human rights progress. He was judged a mediocrity by many legal experts and jurists. His nomination was rejected Apr. 8, 1970, 51-45. For - wrong. Against - right.
Pres. Nixon's veto of urgently-needed hospital construction and modernization funds was overridden June 30, 1970, 76-19. For - right. Against - wrong.

A motion by Sen. Javits (R-N.Y.) to delete the open shop provision in the House version of the postal reform measure so postal employes could be protected by union security agreements was approved June 30, 1970, 52-38. For - right. Against - wrong. (House conservatives subsequently succeeded in barring a union shop.)

The Senate again failed to muster a two-thirds vote to stop a filibuster that has prevented action on a motion to change the Senate rules so that it would only require a three-fifths vote to limit debate and break a filibuster. The majority for invoking cloture and bringing the rules reform to a vote was 55-39 on Mar. 9. This was eight short of a two-thirds vote. For rules reform - right. Against - wrong.

The Senate refused to appropriate funds for the development of a supersonic transport airplane. The AFL-CIO supported funding for the SST in order to revive a depressed aerospace industry and its dwindling work force. The Senate rejected the measure on Mar. 24, 1971 by a 46-51 vote. For - right. Against - wrong.

As one means of improving the economy, the AFL-CIO strongly supported congressional efforts to enact a public service employment program providing jobs for the unemployed in the public sector. The Administration opposed this approach to reducing unemployment as the President had vetoed similar legislation in 1970. The opposition took form in a motion by Sen. Prouty (R-Vt.) which would have in effect killed the measure by recommitting the bill. The motion was defeated by a 29-44 vote on Apr. 1, 1971. For - wrong. Against - right.

Despite continued high unemployment, the Administration opposed a $2 billion accelerated public works program aimed at providing 170,000 jobs and needed facilities in communities with heavy joblessness. Senate efforts to override the Presidential veto on the accelerated public works bill fell five votes short of the necessary two-thirds majority in a 57-36 vote on July 14, 1971. For overriding - right. Against - wrong.

An attempt by Sen. Mathias (R-Md.) to weaken existing federal meat inspection laws by exempting meat products that cross state lines from federal inspection was rejected by the Senate on July 29, 1971 by a 38-52 vote. If passed, this proposal would have left inspection in the hands of weaker state inspection agencies. For - wrong. Against - right.

Some 72,000 jobs were saved by a bill providing federal guarantees on bank loans of $250 million to Lockheed Aircraft Corp. The loan guarantee was narrowly approved on Aug. 2, 1971 by a 49-48 vote. For - right. Against - wrong.

An amendment to the President's tax legislation by Sen. Bayh (D-Ind.) attempted to reduce from 20% to 5% the accelerated depreciation tax write-off for big business and provide instead a one-year tax credit of $25 each to individual taxpayers. The Bayh amendment was narrowly defeated on Nov. 15, 1971 by a 39-40 vote. For - right. Against - wrong.

Carrying the cudgel for the National Right to Work Committee, Sen. Fannin (R-Ariz.) introduced an amendment to deny tax exempt status to any labor organization with a union shop agreement which used any of its income to support or oppose a political candidate. The proposal was rejected Nov. 19, 1971 by a 31-61 vote. For - wrong. Against - right.

By providing for the federal financing of presidential campaign costs the excessive influence of big money on our political system would be effectively reduced. A proposal to this effect was introduced by Sen. Pastore (D-R.I.) as an amendment to the tax law. It would allow taxpayers to voluntarily earmark one dollar of their federal taxes to the presidential campaign of their choice. Although approved by the Senate on Nov. 22, 1971 by a 52-47 vote, the checkoff provision will not take effect until after the 1972 elections. For - right. Against - wrong.

Planning to plow under the family farm, the President nominated Dr. Earl Butz to Secretary of Agriculture. Butz, a leading spokesman for agribusiness, foe of food stamps and consumers, was opposed by the AFL-CIO and most farm groups. He was approved on Dec. 2, 1971 by a 51-44 vote. For - wrong. Against - right.

Continuing his pursuit of an ultra-conservative Supreme Court, Pres. Nixon nominated William H. Rehnquist to fill a vacancy. Rehnquist's unswerving opposition to civil rights and the Bill of Rights marked him as an extremist. A liberal, labor, civil rights coalition opposed his nomination. The nomination however was approved by the Senate Dec. 10, 1971 by a 68-26 vote. For - wrong. Against - right.

Congressional legislation containing a two-year extension of the Office of Economic Opportunity, a separate legal services corporation, and a comprehensive child development program providing voluntary day care services for children of working and welfare mothers was vetoed by Pres. Nixon. The Senate sought to override the veto on Dec. 10, 1971 but fell short of a two-thirds majority with a 51-36 vote. For overriding - right. Against - wrong.

The anti-civil rights forces again surfaced in 1972 during Senate consideration of legislation designed to strengthen the anti-discrimination powers of the Equal Employment Opportunity Commission. In a key vote on Jan. 26, the Senate, by a 46-48 vote, defeated an Administration-supported amendment introduced by Sen. Dominick (R-Colo.) which would have replaced the more expeditious "cease-and-desist" order procedure for preventing job discrimination with a cumbersome and lengthy court enforcement approach. But a subsequent three-week filibuster by opponents of a strong bill forced Senate acceptance of a watered-down version. For - wrong. Against right.

While the Senate was considering legislation to end the West Coast dock strike, Sen. Robert Packwood (R-Ore.) sought to add a compulsory arbitration law for transportation industries. The Senate on Feb. 8 voted 42-39 to table the Packwood amendment, thus killing it. For - right. Against - wrong.

During debate on the hotly controversial busing issue, the Senate approved a labor-supported compromise proposal to allow for the use of busing as a tool to accomplish school desegregation when other methods fail and improved education would result. Prior to this, however, the Senate narrowly rejected an amendment introduced by Sen. Robert Griffin (R-Mich.) which was aimed at prohibiting all forms of busing even to overcome unconstitutional forms of segregation. This amendment was defeated by a 47-50 roll call vote on February 29. For - wrong. Against - right.

Early in the second session, the Senate began debate on legislation designed to increase voter registration and election participation by creating a national voter registration administration that would utilize a computerized postcard registration system. However, Senate Republicans and southern Democrats, fearing increased low-income and black voter participation, strongly opposed passage of this legislation and succeeded on Mar. 15, by a 46-42 vote, in forcing passage of a motion by Sen. James Allen (D-Ala.) to table and thus kill the bill. For - wrong. Against - right.

aflcio_description: An amendment to a child care bill by Sen. Peter H. Dominick (R-Colo.) allowed the Dept. of Health, Education & Welfare to bypass local community groups and channel child care funds to state governments. Despite labor's opposition, the amendment was approved, 35-38, on June 20. For - wrong. Against - right.

During the Senate debate on a Labor-HEW appropriations bill, efforts similar to those in the House were made to seriously weaken the less than-two-year-old Occupational Safety & Health Act. This was the thrust of an amendment exempting firms employing 25 or fewer employes. The Senate rejected this amendment by a 41-44 roll call vote on June 27. For - wrong. Against - right.

corrections: no date printed on the scoreboard; 1972-06-27 per Voteview roll 654
aflcio_description: Following this vote, however, the Senate passed by a 45-41 roll call vote a similar anti-worker amendment introduced again by Curtis which exempted firms employing 15 or fewer workers from coverage under the Act. For - wrong. Against - right.

By a narrow 46-47 vote on July 20, the Senate rejected an effort by conservative Republicans and southern Democrats to scrap a labor-supported bill to raise the minimum wage in steps to $2.20 per hour and extend coverage to millions of other workers. The Administration-backed substitute bill would have provided a lower minimum wage, no extension of coverage and a subminimum youth wage. For - wrong. Against - right.

The AFL-CIO and its maritime affiliates strongly supported legislation requiring that 50 percent of all imported oil not used for fuel or heating purposes be shipped in American-flag vessels. It was estimated that this legislation would generate about 150,000 maritime jobs. The Senate, on July 26, rejected this amendment to the 1973 Maritime Authorization bill by a 33-41 roll call vote. For - right. Against - wrong.

Under heavy pressure from the Administration, trial lawyers and a number of large insurance companies, the Senate voted to scuttle a labor-supported no-fault auto insurance bill. This important consumer legislation, if passed, would have resulted in lower insurance costs through reduced legal fees and better allocation of the premium dollar while providing immediate and full compensation by insurance companies to victims. The legislation was pigeonholed, however, as the Senate agreed by a 49-46 vote on Aug. 8 to refer the bill to the Senate Judiciary Committee for further consideration, in effect killing the proposal. For - wrong. Against - right.

During debate on legislation extending the President's wage-price control authority, a labor-supported amendment freezing interest rates offered by Sen. Thomas McIntyre (D-N.H.) was killed as the Senate on Mar. 20 voted 45-41 for a motion by Sen. Wallace Bennett (R-Utah) to table the amendment. For Tabling - Wrong. Against - Right.

A Senate vote of 60-36 on Apr. 3 was short of the two-thirds needed to override President Nixon's veto of a bill extending and expanding rehabilitation programs for the physically handicapped. For Overriding - Right. Against - Wrong.
A filibuster against a labor-supported bill establishing a nationwide postcard voter registration system was broken on May 9 by a 67-32 vote to close debate. For Cloture - Right. Against - Wrong.

corrections: no date printed on the scoreboard; 1973-05-16 per Voteview roll 135
aflcio_description: The Senate rejected an anti-labor amendment by Senators John Tower (R-Tex.) and Paul Fannin (R-Ariz.) to a bill allowing unions to bargain for the establishment of prepaid legal services plans. Their amendment would have allowed employers to refuse to bargain for this fringe benefit. It was defeated by a 26-66 vote. For - Wrong. Against - Right.

Senators Robert Taft (R-Ohio) and Peter Dominick (R-Colo.) attempted to gut the labor-backed minimum wage bill by stretching the schedule for raising the wage floor, limiting new coverage and overtime protection and imposing a youth subminimum wage rate. The Senate on July 18 rejected this effort by a 40-57 vote. For - Wrong. Against - Right.

A campaign reform bill included a labor-supported provision repealing a technicality in the existing law that appeared to restrict legitimate political action by unions as well as corporations holding government manpower training contracts. An amendment by Sen. William Proxmire (D-Wis.), which would have dropped the labor-supported repealer from the bill, was rejected by a 38-51 vote on July 27. For - Wrong. Against - Right.
An attempt by Sen. Jesse Helms (R-S.C.) to deny food stamps to needy families of strikers was tabled - and thus killed - by a 58-34 vote on July 31. For Tabling - Right. Against - Wrong.

In order to insure nuclear parity with the Soviet Union as provided for under the Strategic Arms Limitation Treaty, the AFL-CIO supported funding of the construction of two Trident nuclear submarines. During debate on the Defense Dept. authorization bill which included funds for this program, Sen. Thomas McIntyre (D-N.H.) offered an amendment which, by cutting Trident funds in half, would have considerably slowed this program. This effort, opposed by organized labor, was defeated by a narrow 47-49 vote on Sept. 27. For - Wrong. Against - Right.

corrections: no date printed on the scoreboard; 1973-12-02 per Voteview roll 527
aflcio_description: A labor-backed amendment which would have provided public financing of presidential elections was killed by a filibuster led by Sen. James Allen (D-Ala.). A key 47-33 vote to halt the filibuster by closing debate was short of the two-thirds required under the Senate's rules. For - Right. Against - Wrong.

Labor supported legislation reorganizing seven bankrupt railroads which included compensation to rail workers displaced or suffering pay cuts because of the reorganization. Sen. J. Glenn Beall (R-Md.) sought to limit payments to workers. The Senate rejected the anti-labor proposal by a 37-59 vote on Dec. 11. For - Wrong. Against - Right.

Consumers would have paid even higher prices if the Senate had approved an amendment by Sen. James Buckley (Cons. R-N.Y.) to deregulate the price of natural gas at the wellhead. It tabled, thus killing, the Buckley amendment by a 45-43 vote on Dec. 19. For Tabling - Right. Against - Wrong.

Amid soaring fuel prices President Nixon vetoed emergency energy powers which included a price rollback for domestic crude oil. On Mar. 6, the Senate by a 58-40 vote failed to obtain the two-thirds vote necessary to override this veto. For override - Right. Against - Wrong.

Although organized labor has strongly endorsed the public financing of federal elections, in the absence of such a system unions must pool the voluntary contributions of their members as a counterbalance to vast individual contributions from those representing big business. On Apr. 3, during debate on an election financing reform bill, the Senate rejected by a 36-53 vote an amendment by Sen. Baker (R-Tenn.) prohibiting unions from collecting voluntary funds for contributions to campaigns. For - Wrong. Against - Right.

Despite heavy pressure from the Administration, trial lawyers, and segments of the insurance industry, the Senate passed legislation setting minimum federal standards for state no-fault auto insurance programs. The bill would cut costs by reducing legal fees, better allocate premium dollars and provide immediate and full compensation by insurance companies to accident victims. The Senate approved the legislation on May 1 by a 53-42 vote. For - Right. Against - Wrong.

With the Administration's wage-price controls controlling only wages while prices, profits and interest rates skyrocketed, organized labor opposed any extension of the President's power to further mismanage the economy. An effort to extend standby control authority and provide for wage-price monitoring was rejected May 1 as the Senate voted 56-32 to table the proposal. For Tabling - Right. Against - Wrong.

corrections: tally 47-41 -> 47-40 per Voteview roll 770
aflcio_description: During debate on NLRA coverage for employes of non-profit hospitals, Sen. Dominick (R-Colo.) offered an amendment that would have seriously weakened the Occupational Safety & Health Act by permitting discretionary rather than mandatory employer penalties for serious safety violations. In a key vote May 7 the Senate tabled this 47-41. For Tabling - Right. Against - Wrong.

The Senate, during debate on the Elementary & Secondary Education bill, rejected an amendment to sharply restrict the Supreme Court's right to provide all children with equal educational opportunity. Sponsored by Sen. Gurney (R-Fla.), the proposal was tabled by a 47-46 vote on May 15. It would have prohibited the busing of children between schools even when no other constitutional remedy was available. For Tabling - Right. Against - Wrong.

During debate on legislation extending the food stamp program, the Senate rejected an amendment by Sen. Helms (R-S.C.) to deny food stamps to needy families of strikers. The amendment was tabled 52-31 on May 21. For Tabling - Right. Against - Wrong.

During debate on a military authorization bill, the Senate rejected an attempt to delete a "safeguard" amendment sponsored by Sen. Jackson (D-Wash.) giving the Secretary of Defense veto power over exports to the Soviet Union when they could be of possible military use. An effort to table this amendment was defeated in a key 40-50 vote June 11. For Tabling - Wrong. Against - Right.

Senate passage of the conference report on legislation extending NLRA protection to workers in non-profit hospitals paved the way for enactment of this long-overdue labor legislation. On July 10 the Senate approved the conference report 64-29. For - Right. Against - Wrong.

In an effort to scuttle the House-passed Consumer Protection Agency, anti-consumer senators sought to treat labor as a commodity by placing labor-management relations within the new agency's jurisdiction. The amendment was tabled by the Senate 49-42 on July 16. For Tabling - Right. Against - Wrong.

The Senate passed a so-called "emergency" strike bill affecting West Coast maritime trade with Hawaii and other Pacific Islands that would permit island officials or employers to obtain a 160-day injunction over and above the 80-day cooling-off period provided under the 1947 Taft-Hartley Act. A labor-supported attempt by Sen. Javits (R-N.Y.) to recommit and thus kill the bill failed by a 31-65 vote July 17. For Recommittal - Right. Against - Wrong.

aflcio_description: At the start of the 94th Congress, labor and civil rights groups again supported efforts to liberalize the Senate's rule for ending filibusters. As in previous years, the first major procedural hurdle was whether a new Senate - before adopting its rules - could end debate by a simple majority vote. Sen. Pearson (R-Kan.) moved to close debate on a proposed change in the filibuster rule and Sen. Mansfield (D-Mont.) raised a point-of-order against the motion to bring the issue to a vote. When the Senate on Feb. 15 approved, 51-42, a motion by Sen. Mondale (D-Minn.) to table the Mansfield point of order, the Senate affirmed its right to close debate by majority vote at the beginning of a new Congress. This key vote eventually led to a change in the filibuster rule, whereby cloture could be obtained with 60 votes. For tabling - Right. Against tabling - Wrong.

The AFL-CIO has long sought revisions in the tax code to permit the fair taxation of profits earned by U.S.-based multinational companies. In Senate debate on a multi-billion-dollar tax reduction bill, Sen. Hartke (D-Ind.) sponsored an amendment to partially close this loophole. His proposal would repeal the foreign tax credit on all foreign oil-related income, making it instead a deduction while providing that such oil related income be taxed at a 24 percent tax rate. An effort by Sen. Curtis (R-Neb.) to table this labor-backed proposal was rejected by 44-52 on Mar. 19. This defeat paved the way for inclusion of the Hartke provision in the tax bill later passed by the Senate. The provision was, however, watered down in the final conference report on the tax rebate bill eventually signed into law. For tabling - Wrong. Against tabling - Right.

During earlier Senate consideration of the omnibus energy bill, efforts were similarly made to end oil price controls. A heated battle took place on an amendment by Sen. Johnston (D-La.) to decontrol prices on oil from existing wells recovered by secondary and tertiary means. An effort by Sen. Jackson (D-Wash.) to table the proposal was rejected 42-45 on Apr. 9. The failure of this tabling motion led to the eventual partial decontrol of this oil. For - Right. Against - Wrong.
